strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 10 watermarking schemes, 5 model sizes, and multiple text lengths with strong experimental documentation
Well-motivated theoretical framework (adaptive robustness radius) that provides principled perspective on watermark security, with formal Theorem 1 guaranteeing KL-constrained robustness
Important practical insights: system prompts significantly boost attacks (understudied in prior work), reasoning capability degrades watermark resilience, long-form robustness is weaker than claimed
Striking empirical results: 98.5% ESR with only 100 training samples and zero detector access substantially exceeds prior work (GPT-4o: 6.75%)
Extensive reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and thorough ablations (OOD generalization, mixed-key training, training set size sensitivity)
Detection score distribution analysis (Figure 4b) demonstrates RLCracker aligns paraphrased outputs with unwatermarked distributions, not just erasing watermarks
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Adaptive robustness radius (Theorem 1) provides bounds on expected scores but the practical RL objective (Eq. 1) doesn't explicitly optimize this radius; connection between minimizing theoretical objective and empirical success is indirect
Assumption 1 (sub-Gaussian detector score) is strong and unvalidated empirically for complex schemes like SIR/X-SIR; violation of this assumption invalidates theoretical guarantees

Critical hyperparameter sensitivity: RLCracker requires different weight configurations (w₁, w₂, w₃) per watermarking scheme (Table 7) and is highly sensitive (Figure 5), but paper doesn't address how attackers determine optimal weights without detector access, undermining 'detector-free' claims
Reference model choice for Ph (using base model πref) is somewhat circular and lacks rigorous justification; unclear why base model adequately proxies human-like text
P-SP semantic similarity threshold (0.7) is arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; median P-SP ranges 0.75-0.95 across conditions, so threshold changes could materially affect conclusions

Training data accessibility understudied: 100 watermarked samples requires either repeated generator queries or detector access/side information; practical feasibility in real-world settings is unclear
Limited algorithmic novelty: RLCracker uses standard GRPO with semantic+KL rewards; the main contribution is empirical evaluation rather than methodological innovation

Unigram watermark shows lower ESR (67-98.5%) than other schemes but paper provides no analysis of why RLCracker struggles with certain watermark properties or what design characteristics make attacks harder
No direct comparison with concurrent work B⁴ across full set of watermarks; limited to single model in Table 1
Ethical concerns underexplored: no mention of responsible disclosure to watermark developers, no discussion of coordinated disclosure timeline, no analysis of misuse prevention

strengths: Novel theoretical framework (adaptive robustness radius) bridging certified robustness to watermarking, with practical KL-divergence approximation and formal lower bound (Theorem 4.3)
Impressive practical efficiency: achieves 98.5% watermark removal with only 100 training samples, zero detector access, and minimal computational requirements (0.5-1.5 hours)

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 10 watermarking schemes, 5 model sizes, multiple text lengths with thorough ablations on training data, mixed-key robustness, and cross-model transfer
Valuable practical insights about overlooked vulnerabilities: system prompts, reasoning capabilities, and test-time scaling that are actionable for watermark designers
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, standard toolkit usage, clear experimental protocols, and promised code release
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: adaptive robustness radius nominally requires detector access yet threat model claims zero access; KL radius is a lower bound on an already-relaxed notion, making tightness guarantees unclear

Poor cross-watermark transferability undermines claimed broad effectiveness: training on one watermark (EWD) achieves only 13.3% ESR on Unigram vs. 67% Base, limiting applicability when watermark type unknown
Limited defensive guidance: paper excels at attack but provides minimal analysis of watermark design principles that confer robustness or recommendations beyond increasing embedding strength

Reference distribution approximation concerns: P_h approximated via model rather than human text; Table 13 shows high sensitivity to proxy choice (91.5% → 57% ESR), and Appendix D.16 validation shows persistent distribution gaps

Semantic similarity metric limitations: P-SP score is relatively simple without human evaluation validation; threshold (0.7) appears arbitrary with high sensitivity shown in Figure 7; some outputs show fluency degradation (PPL 2.83 on XSIR vs. 3.11 baseline)
